title: I think, and the numbers say
summary: Learn what turns an opinion into evidence, build a constructive where every point has to carry a number you can point at, then defend it in a full round against a grown up who will ask where each number came from.
materials: the two totals your cost sheet program printed this week, on paper or on screen
the v0.2 sketch with its real prices and receipts
a grown up to take the other side

steps.title: The difference between I think and the numbers say
steps.body:
Two sentences, and a judge hears them completely differently.

I think our stand will make money.

The materials for one unit cost 3 dollars, the sign board cost 12 dollars once, and at ten units that is 42 dollars of costs against whatever we take in.

The first sentence is a wish with a person attached. The second one can be checked, argued with, and beaten, and that is exactly why it is stronger. Anyone can disagree with what you think. To disagree with the second sentence they have to come after your numbers, and if your numbers are honest they will not get far.

So from this week your points have three parts, not two. Claim, then reason, then evidence. The claim is what you want believed. The reason is why it follows. The evidence is the thing outside your own head that makes the reason stand up.

What counts as evidence: a number you measured yourself, a price you actually paid with a receipt behind it, a thing that visibly happened, or a number from somewhere you can name out loud. What does not count: a feeling, a guess with a number's clothes on, a number you cannot say the source of, and the word obviously. If you cannot finish the sentence I know that because, then what you are holding is not evidence yet.

This is exactly why Build spent the hour splitting your money into two pockets. You now own numbers that nobody handed you. Use them, and say where each one came from as you use it: my receipt, my cost sheet, my sketch.

The steelman rule is still standing and it gets harder this week: before you argue, say the other side's best point back so well that they nod, and if their best point has a number in it, say the number too, not just the mood of it.

And the question of the week to carry into your recording at the end: what makes a price fair? You are about to set one on a real thing, so this is not a school question this time.

steps.title: Build a constructive that cannot be waved away
steps.body:
The motion is: allowance should be earned, not given. Pick the side you actually believe, then earn it.

Three points, one index card each. On the front of the card write the claim in one line. Under it write the reason in one line, beginning with the word because. Under that write the evidence, and under the evidence write where it came from.

One of your three points has to carry a real number out of your own week, and it has to be a number you can point at, not remember. The two totals your cost sheet program printed are the obvious ones: what a unit really eats in materials, and what the once only costs came to. Your receipts and your v0.2 sketch work too. If the program did not run today, use a price straight off a receipt and say it is off a receipt. What is not allowed is a number you made up in the last minute to make a sentence sound heavier.

Signpost the whole thing so a listener never has to guess where you are: my first point, my second point, my third point, and after each claim, the words and here is how I know.

Then turn the timer over and deliver it standing, twice. Two minutes is the whole speech, so a point that eats a minute has stolen from the other two. If you run over, cut sentences from the point you like most, because that is where the extra words hide.

Last, before the round starts, do the steelman out loud: say the best point the other side has, with its number if it has one, and say it as if you meant it.
checklist: Three index cards, each with a claim, a because reason, an evidence line, and where that evidence came from
At least one point carries a real number from my own week and I can put my finger on where it is written
No point rests on a number I cannot name the source of out loud
I signposted each point and said the words here is how I know before every piece of evidence
I delivered it standing twice inside the two minute timer, and I steelmanned the other side before the round began

steps.title: Record it
steps.prompt: Record your two minute constructive in one take, standing, cards in hand, holding up the piece of paper your number came from when you reach it. Then, in the same recording, answer this week's question: what makes a price fair, and what is your reason? Say whether your answer changed after you saw what one of your own units actually costs to make.
